traditions/universal-church-of-the-kingd: Universal Church of the Kingdom of God

Founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977 by Edir Macedo. A neo-Pentecostal church emphasising deliverance from evil spirits, healing and prosperity through sacrificial giving, it built the vast Temple of Solomon in São Paulo (2014), owns the RecordTV network and is linked to the Republicanos party. It has faced investigations and conflicts in several countries (e.g. the 2019–21 schism and expulsion of Brazilian bishops in Angola), which the church contests; critics also cite hostility to Afro-Brazilian religions.
Deliverance sessions confronting spirits (often identified with Afro-Brazilian deities)
Scripture as interpreted by the church's leadership.
Faith in Christ expressed through sacrifice and confrontation of evil; healing and prosperity as signs.
Baptism by immersion and the Lord's Supper.
Expectation of Christ's return; little emphasis compared with present deliverance.
Centralised episcopal hierarchy under the founding bishop.
Daily themed services (prosperity, healing, family, deliverance).
traditions/vineyard/summary: A movement begun with Kenneth Gulliksen's Vineyard Fellowship (1974) and shaped from 1982 by John Wimber, a former Calvary Chapel pastor. Wimber taught 'power evangelism' and the 'Third Wave' of the Spirit, combining evangelical theology with healing and prophecy while avoiding Pentecostal labels. The Vineyard released the Toronto Airport congregation in 1995 over the 'Toronto Blessing'. Vineyard worship songs shaped global contemporary worship.
traditions/vineyard/distinctives/0: Kingdom theology (George Eldon Ladd's 'already and not yet')
traditions/vineyard/distinctives/1: 'Everyone gets to play' — ministry by all believers
traditions/vineyard/profile/authority: Scripture as the final authority; Vineyard Statement of Faith.
traditions/vineyard/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace through faith; ongoing filling of the Spirit without tongues as required evidence.
traditions/vineyard/profile/governance: Association of churches with national movements; senior pastors.
traditions/vineyard/profile/worship: Extended intimate worship followed by teaching and ministry time.
traditions/calvary-chapel/summary: Began when Chuck Smith, formerly a Foursquare pastor, took over a small church in Costa Mesa, California, in 1965 and welcomed hippies of the Jesus Movement with the help of Lonnie Frisbee. It pioneered contemporary Christian music (Maranatha! Music), verse-by-verse Bible teaching and mass beach baptisms. Calvary Chapel describes itself as a middle way between fundamentalism and Pentecostal emotionalism.
traditions/calvary-chapel/profile/author: Scripture as inerrant; no denominational confession beyond Calvary Chapel distinctives.
traditions/calvary-chapel/profile/sacram: Believers' baptism (often in the ocean) and communion.
traditions/calvary-chapel/profile/govern: Senior pastor with board; loose fellowship of affiliated churches (two associations since 2016).
traditions/hillsong/summary: Founded in 1983 as Hills Christian Life Centre in Sydney by Brian and Bobbie Houston within the Assemblies of God in Australia; renamed Hillsong in 1999. Its worship music became among the most widely sung in the world, and it planted large churches in global cities. It left the Australian Christian Churches in 2018. From 2020 scandals involving leaders led to the departure of many campuses and Brian Houston's resignation (2022); he was acquitted in 2023 of concealing his father's abuse.
traditions/hillsong/distinctives/2: Pentecostal theology with polished contemporary presentation
traditions/hillsong/profile/salvation: Salvation by grace; Spirit-filled life and flourishing.
traditions/hillsong/profile/governance: Global senior pastors with a board.
traditions/hillsong/profile/worship: Concert-style worship with professional music production.
traditions/bethel-new-apostolic-networks: Bethel Church (Redding) and New Apostolic Reformation networks

A loose constellation of independent charismatic networks led by self-described apostles and prophets. C. Peter Wagner popularised the term 'New Apostolic Reformation' in the 1990s for what he saw as the restoration of apostolic governance. Bethel Church in Redding, California, led by Bill Johnson since 1996, left the Assemblies of God in 2006 and became influential through its supernatural ministry school and worship music. Many participants reject the NAR label; critics raise concerns about extra-biblical revelation and the political 'Seven Mountains' mandate.
'Kingdom now' theology of heaven invading earth
Scripture as final authority, with emphasis on ongoing prophetic revelation.
Salvation by grace; believers called to exercise supernatural power.
Optimistic, often victorious or postmillennial-leaning eschatology.
Relational apostolic networks without formal denominational structures.
Long worship sets, prophetic ministry and healing prayer.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/summary: The Church of Jesus Christ on Earth through the Prophet Simon Kimbangu traces its origin to Kimbangu's healing ministry at Nkamba in the Belgian Congo in 1921. Arrested within months, Kimbangu died in prison in 1951 while his followers were deported and persecuted. The church was legally recognised in 1959, joined the World Council of Churches in 1969 and is among Africa's largest independent churches. Later teaching that exalted Simon Kimbangu and his successors, including identification of Kimbangu with the Holy Spirit, has strained relations with other Congolese Protestant churches.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/distinctiv: Strict ethics: no alcohol, tobacco, pork or violence
traditions/kimbanguist-church/profile/au: Scripture, with the revelations of Simon Kimbangu and his successors.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/profile/sa: Salvation in Christ, mediated through obedience and the prophetic ministry.
Baptism by laying on of hands (without water) and communion with locally produced elements.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/profile/es: Expectation of judgment and renewal centred on the holy city of Nkamba.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/profile/go: Spiritual heads drawn from Kimbangu's family.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/profile/wo: Brass bands, choirs, prayers and pilgrimage to Nkamba.
traditions/kimbanguist-church/status: Active; millions of adherents in the DRC and neighbouring countries.
traditions/zion-christian-church/summary: Founded by Engenas Lekganyane about 1924 in the northern Transvaal, from the 'Zionist' movement that grew from the Christian Catholic Church of John Alexander Dowie (Zion, Illinois) through South African leaders. The ZCC, headquartered at Moria in Limpopo, is the largest church in southern Africa; its Easter pilgrimage draws over a million people. It combines Christian faith with healing through blessed water and other objects and with African ways of life.
traditions/zion-christian-church/distinc: Healing through prayer, blessed water, tea and cords
Star and dove badges worn by members
Prohibition of alcohol, tobacco and pork
traditions/zion-christian-church/profile: Scripture as read and applied by the bishop.
Salvation and healing in Christ, protection from evil and wholeness of life.
Baptism by triple immersion and Holy Communion.
Expectation of God's Kingdom; focus on present wellbeing.
Hereditary bishop with ministers and preachers.
Dancing, singing, uniforms and testimony; pilgrimage.
traditions/zion-christian-church/status: Active; the largest independent church in southern Africa.
traditions/church-of-the-lord-aladura/su: Founded in 1930 at Ogere, Nigeria, by Josiah Olunowo Ositelu, a former Anglican catechist who received visions. One of the Yoruba 'praying' (Aladura) churches, it uses prayer, fasting, holy names and prophecy for healing and protection, and spread to Ghana, Liberia, Sierra Leone and Britain. It joined the World Council of Churches in 1975.
traditions/church-of-the-lord-aladura/di: Prayer as central practice (aladura = "owners of prayer")
Holy names and sacred seals revealed to the founder
traditions/church-of-the-lord-aladura/pr: Scripture with revelations given to the founder and prophets.
Salvation in Christ, experienced as healing, protection and power through prayer.
Primate and hierarchy of bishops, prophets and apostles.
White-robed worship, barefoot, with drumming, prayer and ecstatic prophecy.
traditions/celestial-church-of-christ/su: Founded at Porto-Novo, Dahomey (now Benin), in 1947 by Samuel Bilewu Oshoffa after a vision during an eclipse. A prophetic-healing church related to the Aladura family, it spread rapidly in Nigeria and the West African diaspora. Members worship in white garments, barefoot, and observe purity rules.
traditions/celestial-church-of-christ/di: Visions and prophecy guiding church life
White soutanes and bare feet in worship
Rejection of traditional charms and idols
traditions/celestial-church-of-christ/pr: Scripture with the revelations given to the founder.
Salvation in Christ, protection from evil, healing.
Baptism by immersion and Holy Communion.
Pastor-founder succeeded by Pastors; hierarchy of ranks.
Liturgy with chanting, candles, incense and prophetic visions.
traditions/celestial-church-of-christ/st: Active; succession disputes have produced rival factions since 1985.
traditions/nazareth-baptist-church/summa: Founded in 1910 in Natal by the Zulu prophet Isaiah Shembe, who had been associated with the African Native Baptist Church. Centred on the holy village of Ekuphakameni and the mountain Nhlangakazi, it blends biblical faith with Zulu culture and Sabbath observance. Many members regard Shembe as a divinely sent prophet or messianic figure, a view outsiders and members interpret differently. It has divided among Shembe's descendants.
traditions/nazareth-baptist-church/profi: Scripture, especially the Old Testament, with the hymns and revelations of the Shembe prophets.
Salvation through God revealed in Christ and in the prophet Shembe.
Baptism and Holy Communion (including a night communion with feet washing).
Expectation of judgment and divine restoration.
Leadership by successors of Isaiah Shembe.
Hymn-singing and sacred dance on Sabbath and festivals.
traditions/harrist-church/summary: Communities formed in Côte d'Ivoire by converts of the Liberian prophet William Wade Harris (1913–15), who baptised tens of thousands and told them to wait for 'teachers with Bibles'. Many joined the Methodist mission; others organised under John Ahui, whom Harris commissioned in 1928, into the Harrist Church, officially recognised in the 1950s.
traditions/harrist-church/distinctives/0: Founder's call to burn fetishes and turn to the one God
traditions/harrist-church/profile/author: Scripture as proclaimed by Harris; oral tradition of his teaching.
traditions/harrist-church/profile/salvat: Turning to God and away from idols, with baptism.
traditions/harrist-church/profile/govern: Preachers and apostles with a central council.
traditions/harrist-church/profile/worshi: Singing in local languages and preaching in white robes.
